raw_case_text: A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted (Figure 1A and B ), papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections (Figure 1C). The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative. A skin biopsy imprint revealed amastigotes. Skin culture in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle medium grew promastigotes characterized as Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis by isoenzymes. The leishmanin skin test was positive. Bacterial superinfection of the ulcers was treated with cephalexin. Because of a contraindication to treatment with pentavalent antimony (individual > 50 years of age), and lack of medical infrastructure where he lived for providing amphotericin B, the patient was treated with oral fluconazole, 9 mg/kg per day. Over the following 6-month period of treatment, the lesions healed completely, many leaving no scars (Figure 1D). Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis is an uncommon presentation of Leishmania (V.) braziliensis infection. Most of the lesions are thought to be due to bloodstream dissemination, not to multiple sand fly bites. The reason that some people develop disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis is not fully understood.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of widely disseminated skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 52-year-old male farm worker presented with a 4-month history of widespread skin lesions that initially erupted on the face and lower extremities before disseminating over most of his body surface, including the genitalia, soles, and scalp. He reported experiencing daily fevers during the first two weeks of the illness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident and farm worker in Ceará state, northeast Brazil. Prior chronic illnesses and previous antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Daily fever during the initial two weeks of illness; widespread skin eruptions. Denied weight loss, night sweats, arthralgias, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed 178 skin lesions of varying morphology: ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular, distributed on the face, trunk, limbs, genitalia, soles of the feet, and scalp. Multiple ulcers demonstrated clinical evidence of secondary bacterial superinfection. Remainder of physical examination was within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and liver function tests were within normal reference ranges. Serological testing for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy imprint examination under light microscopy demonstrated intracellular microorganisms within phagocytic cells. In vitro fungal/protozoal cultures established.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (DL) caused by Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis, complicated by secondary bacterial pyoderma.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Skin biopsy imprint revealed Leishmania amastigotes. Skin culture in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) medium grew promastigotes characterized as Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis by isoenzyme analysis. Montenegro (leishmanin) skin test was positive.
Differentials Ruled Out: Secondary syphilis, disseminated histoplasmosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, leprosy, and HIV-associated cutaneous manifestations.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Secondary bacterial wound infection was treated with oral cephalexin. Because pentavalent antimony was contraindicated due to age (> 50 years) and infrastructure for amphotericin B was unavailable, oral fluconazole was initiated at 9 mg/kg/day. Over a 6-month treatment course, all 178 lesions completely healed, many without scarring.
